title: The Yugoslav set-up: what every move prepares, and the move-order questions
outcomes: Says in one sentence what each early move of the Yugoslav set-up prepares: the pawn on f3 (support for e4, then g4), the queen on d2 (guard for e3, long castling, the h6 diagonal), the bishop's square on c4, long castling
Says what each early Black move prepares: the bishop on g7, castling, the knight on c6, the bishop on d7 and the rook on c8
Checks the conditions before the bishop trade on h6 (count the defenders of d4) and before ...d5 (count the controllers of d5)
Compares move orders: three roads to one position, and what the slow seventh moves (Qd2, Be2) allow Black to do
Names typical mistakes for both sides and the engine's verdict on each, and reads master counts as choices, not verdicts

steps.prompt: Before any explanation, one sentence each, even if you are not sure: what job does the pawn on f3 do? What job does the queen on d2 do? You will come back to your answers at the end.

steps.text: **The question of this lesson.** The Yugoslav set-up is a chain of promises: each early move is a loan that a later move repays. By the end you can say, for each move, what it prepares. For White: the f-pawn, the queen, the bishop's square, long castling. For Black: the bishop on g7, castling, the knight, the bishop on d7, the rook on c8. You will also judge when the order matters. Emanuel Lasker is said to have urged naming each move's purpose (our synthesis sheet). [S]

steps.text: **Idea 1: support the pawn on e4.** White's pawn on e4 is attacked by Black's knight on f6 and held only by the knight on c3. The pawn on f3 is the second defender, and it also takes g4 away from Black's knight. [I] Of all the moves in the set-up, f3 is the least natural for a beginner: it takes the f3 square from the knight on d4 and loosens the king. Treat it as a price White pays on purpose.

steps.text: **The price of f3.** Edward Lasker advised asking which squares a pawn push stops guarding (our synthesis sheet; he meant pawns near a castled king, so here it applies by analogy). [S][I] The pawn on f2 guarded e3 and g3. On f3 it guards e4 and g4 instead, takes the knight's retreat square, and leaves the bishop on e3 with no pawn behind it. That is why the queen comes to d2 next: it takes over the guard of e3. One loan, one repayment.

steps.text: **Idea 3: Black has castled, so White castles long.** Capablanca advised delaying castling until the opponent's plan is known. [S] Black's king is already on g8, which is a reason to prefer long castling, not a rule. [I] Why not castle short? The bishop on f1 still blocks the way, and a king on g1 would stand where White's own pawns are about to advance. [I] Qd2, the bishop on e3 and the empty squares b1, c1 and d1 prepared long castling.

steps.text: **What slowness gives away.** Emanuel Lasker asked that each opening move add working power; Nimzowitsch, by our synthesis sheet, stressed the whole army working together. [S] By that test the early queen move is slow: it gives Black ...Ng4 and the evaluation falls from a small White edge to level. The bishop to e2 is slow in another way: it lets ...d5 work. [I] Each option Black keeps open is an option White keeps too, so flexibility has a price for both.

steps.prompt: Do you agree that every option Black keeps open is also an option for White? Try to find a counterexample from the boards you have seen. [I] This is my inference, not a proven rule.

steps.text: **Why f3 works, and when it stops.** f3 holds up e4 and g4 as long as pawns stand on those squares. After ...d5 and the exchange of e4, the pawn on f3 guards two empty squares and takes the knight's retreat square. [H] It may do less work than before, but the engine still prefers White, by roughly half a pawn or more, so this is a reduction in value, not a mistake. Look at the exchange on the next board.

steps.text: **Two good plans, not one necessity.** The engine's first choice is long castling at once, then the bishop to c4, then the pawn storm; at depth 16 both stand roughly +0.5 to +0.9 for White, varying by run. [V] After ...d5 White still stands better. Why castle before c4? [H] The bishop on c4 can be chased by a knight to a5 and a rook to c8, while castling brings a rook to d1 straight away. Treat c4 as one good plan, not a requirement.

**Typical mistakes.** For Black: jumping with the knight to g4 while White's queen still stands on d1. For White: trading bishops on h6 while the knight on d4 needs the bishop; a slow pawn move (a3) or the bishop to d3, which let ...d5 work. The next boards check each one with the engine.

steps.text:
**What to remember.**
- f3 pays for e4 and g4; it costs e3, g3 and f3.
- Qd2 guards e3, clears d1, later sees h6.
- No short castling yet: f1 blocks it and the pawn storm comes. [I]
